newsitem.title: CHINA: Foreign, local makers aim for China TV market.
newsitem.headline: Foreign, local makers aim for China TV market.

text.p: Foreign and local Chinese TV production firms gathered on Friday for Shanghai's sixth annual international television festival, aiming to sell programmes to one of world's fastest growing markets.
More than 600 companies from 37 countries and regions have come for the festival from November 9 to 14, which gives them a chance to meet potential buyers from all over the country, organisers said.

China's television market is huge. It has 3,000 television stations, a third of which are educational channels, a third cable channels and a third air-to-air channels. The nation boasts more than 300 million sets and a penetration rate of more than 90 percent in urban areas.
"China in economic terms is going to become the biggest economic force in the world," said Peter Kraewinkels, of the European Association of Television Programme Distributors.
"Television will follow. It must become the biggest television market in production and broadcast hours within 10 years, without any doubt," he said in an interview.

But European firms trail Asian and North American competitors, with total sales to China of 1,000 hours worth only $1 million in 1996, with some producers put off by copyright problems and what they see as an unclear and insecure business environment, Kraewinkels said.

"The Chinese are very good at protecting their market," he said. "They say there is no quota. We assume there are quotas on hours and titles they can buy but nobody (among the authorities) will confirm this."

Ye Zhikang, director-general of the Radio, Film and Television Bureau of Shanghai, told reporters there was no quota on foreign programmes shown on Chinese channels. "It is up to each television station and each region to decide."
Channels obtain foreign programmes through direct purchase, exchange of programmes or allowing the seller to pre-sell advertising space in them, he said.
He said China would not allow programmes with excess violence or sex, or which were unhelpful to China's development and people.
As of the end of 1995, China's cable television stations served nearly 200 million people and the number is expected to grow to 300 million by the year 2000, official figures show.

China's biggest cable television station is in Shanghai, with 1.8 million subscribers and estimated 1996 advertising revenue of 200 million yuan ($24 million), up from 130 million in 1995 and 60 million in 1994, said Chen Wen, head of its editorial office.

Chen said in an interview that her company preferred programmes from the Chinese-speaking world that were closer to the thinking and lifestyle of Chinese but also welcomed European and American documentaries and special programmes.
Her station has five channels and plans to add a sixth shopping channel in 1997, she said. It carries programmes from the U.S. sports channel ESPN and cartoons made by Turner Broadcasting.
"Our basic policy is to make as few programmes as possible," she said. "It is cheaper to buy, than make programmes."
